h: Why your EMI goes up when RBI sneezes 🤧
m: The interest rate at which the RBI lends money to banks for a short time.
e: When the RBI raises the repo rate, banks borrow at a higher cost. So the EMI on Priya's home loan from her bank goes up too.
i: "A repo rate cut usually makes loans cheaper, which can push up demand for cars and homes."
tm: Banks park money with the RBI.
y: "Repo" is short for "repurchase": the borrower sells securities and agrees to buy them back. From Latin re- (again) + Old French purchacier (to seek, obtain).

h: Buying gold this Dhanteras? There's a smarter way 🪙
m: A fund that tracks the price of gold and trades on the stock exchange like a share.
e: Instead of buying a gold coin, Priya buys Gold ETF units worth Rs 2,000 through her demat account. No locker, no making charges.
i: "Gold ETFs let people invest in gold without storage or purity worries."
y: "ETF" stands for Exchange Traded Fund. "Exchange" comes from Old French eschangier (to change); "fund" from Latin fundus (bottom, foundation).

h: Why the stock market opens for 1 hour on Diwali 🪔
m: A special one-hour stock trading session held on Diwali evening, seen as a lucky start to the new year.
e: Every Diwali, NSE and BSE open for about an hour in the evening, and many families buy a few shares for good luck.
i: "Muhurat trading is more about tradition than big profits, but it gets many first-time investors started."
y: "Muhurat" comes from Sanskrit muhūrta, an auspicious moment of time. It names the special trading hour held on Diwali.

h: Why you pick one brand over ten others 🎯
m: The one clear reason customers choose your product over every other option.
e: Domino's built its name in India on a simple promise: pizza delivered in 30 minutes.
i: "Before launching, I would define the USP in one line a customer can repeat."
y: "USP" stands for Unique Selling Proposition. The phrase was coined in the 1940s by Rosser Reeves of the US advertising agency Ted Bates & Co.

f: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation & Amortisation
h: Your company looks rich. One word knows the truth. 👀
m: The profit a business makes from its daily work, before paying loans, taxes and wear and tear.
e: Raju's chai stall earns Rs 50,000 a month and spends Rs 35,000 on milk, tea, sugar and his helper. His EBITDA is Rs 15,000.
i: "Their EBITDA margin is rising, so the core business is becoming more efficient."
y: An acronym of Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortisation. "Amortise" comes from Old French amortir (to deaden, extinguish), from Latin mors (death): the debt is slowly killed off.

h: People leave managers, not companies. There's a word for it.
m: The rate at which employees leave a company and are not replaced right away.
e: If 20 out of 100 employees leave a company in a year, its attrition rate is 20%.
i: "High attrition costs money, because hiring and training new people is expensive."
y: From Latin attritio, "a rubbing away" (ad- + terere, to rub). Staff wear away from a company slowly, like stone rubbed smooth.

h: ₹10 samosa became ₹20. Blame this word. 🥟
m: The steady rise in prices over time, so the same money buys less.
e: A samosa that cost Rs 10 a few years ago now costs Rs 20 in many college canteens. Your Rs 100 buys fewer samosas.
i: "When inflation is high, the RBI often raises interest rates to slow it down."
y: From Latin inflare, "to blow into" (in- + flare, to blow). Prices swell like a balloon being blown up.

h: Startups don't die of failure. They die of this. 🔥
m: How much cash a startup spends every month more than it earns.
e: A startup with Rs 60 lakh in the bank and a burn rate of Rs 5 lakh a month has about 12 months left.
i: "I would track burn rate monthly, so the team knows how much runway is left."
y: "Burn" comes from Old English beornan. Startup slang from the 1990s for how fast a company "burns" through its cash.

h: Free to start. Paid to stay. Smart, right? 😏
m: A product that is free to use, with extra features for people who pay.
e: Music apps let you listen free with ads, and remove the ads if you pay for the premium plan.
i: "Freemium works when enough free users love the product and upgrade."
tm: Everything free, for a few days.
y: A blend of "free" and "premium", popularised around 2006 by venture capitalist Fred Wilson and named by Jarid Lukin.

h: Same product. Higher price. People still buy. Why? 🤔
m: The extra value a brand name adds, which makes people trust it and pay more for it.
e: Many families pick Amul butter without even checking other brands. That trust is brand equity.
i: "Strong brand equity lets a company charge a premium and launch new products easily."
y: "Brand" comes from Old English brand (fire, burning), as in the mark burned onto cattle to show the owner. "Equity" comes from Latin aequitas (fairness), later meaning an owner's share of value.

h: 4 years. ₹5 lakh on a degree. What's the ROI? 🎓
m: How much you gain compared with what you spent, usually shown as a percentage.
e: You spend Rs 10,000 on a stall at a college fest and earn Rs 15,000. Your ROI is 50%.
i: "Before any campaign, I would estimate the ROI so we know it is worth the spend."
y: An acronym of Return on Investment. "Invest" comes from Latin investire (to clothe, surround): money is "dressed" in an asset.

h: Your first week decides if you stay a year. 🗓️
m: The way a company welcomes and trains a new employee so they settle in quickly.
e: On day one, a new hire gets a laptop, a buddy, a training plan and lunch with the team. That is good onboarding.
i: "Good onboarding reduces early attrition because new hires feel welcome."
y: From "on board", originally a ship's term for being aboard. It came into HR use in the 1970s and 80s for bringing new employees into an organisation.

h: One number tells how a whole country is doing. 🇮🇳
m: The total value of all goods and services a country produces in a year.
e: Every chai sold, every car made and every haircut given in India adds to India's GDP.
i: "Faster GDP growth usually means more jobs and higher incomes."
y: An acronym of Gross Domestic Product. "Gross" comes from Old French gros (large, whole), meaning a total before deductions; "domestic" from Latin domus (home).

h: ₹50 lakh for 10%. So what's the company worth? 🦈
m: What a company is worth, usually worked out when investors buy a share in it.
e: If an investor pays Rs 50 lakh for 10% of a startup, the startup's valuation is Rs 5 crore.
i: "A high valuation is good news, but the company must grow fast to justify it."
y: From Old French valoir, from Latin valere (to be strong, be worth).

h: Your phone just replaced your bank queue. 📱
m: Technology that makes money services like payments, loans and investing easier.
e: Paying the canteen with UPI in two seconds is fintech in action.
i: "Fintech has brought banking to people in small towns who never visited a bank branch."
y: A blend of "financial technology". The word appeared in the 1990s and spread widely after about 2014.

h: "Only 2 left in stock!" Ever wondered why? 👀
m: Making a product feel limited, so people buy quickly before they miss out.
e: Shopping apps show "Only 2 left" or a sale timer counting down, so you buy now instead of thinking.
i: "Scarcity works, but brands must use it honestly or customers lose trust."
y: "Scarcity" comes from Old French escars (scanty), from Latin excarpsus (picked out). "Marketing" comes from Latin mercatus (trade, market).

h: Profitable but no cash? This is why. 💸
m: The money a business has for daily needs: what it owns now minus what it owes soon.
e: A kirana shop needs cash to stock shelves before customers pay. That cash is its working capital.
i: "Even a profitable company can struggle if its working capital is too low."
y: "Capital" comes from Latin capitalis (of the head, chief), from caput (head), also the root of "cattle", an early measure of wealth.

h: Your boss judges you on 3 or 4 things. Know them. 🎯
m: The main areas a person is responsible for and judged on in their job.
e: A sales executive's KRAs could be monthly sales, new clients and customer follow-ups.
i: "In my first week, I would ask my manager to clarify my KRAs."
y: An acronym of Key Result Area, a term from management-by-objectives thinking in the second half of the 20th century.

h: The government spends more than it earns. Then what? 🏛️
m: When a government spends more than it earns in a year, the gap it must borrow to fill.
e: Every Union Budget announces a fiscal deficit target, shown as a percentage of India's GDP.
i: "A lower fiscal deficit means the government needs to borrow less."
y: "Fiscal" comes from Latin fiscus, the basket in which Roman tax money was kept. "Deficit" is Latin for "it is lacking".

h: Plan A failed. The smart ones do this. 🔄
m: When a startup changes its main idea or customer, based on what it has learnt.
e: Paytm began as a mobile recharge service and later grew into a full payments company.
i: "A pivot is not failure. It means listening to the market."
tm: Keep going on the same path.
y: From French pivot, the pin on which something turns. Eric Ries made it popular in startups (The Lean Startup, 2011) for a change of direction.

h: Why everyone you know is on the same app. 🌐
m: When a product becomes more useful as more people use it.
e: UPI is useful because almost every shop accepts it. The more people use it, the more useful it becomes.
i: "Network effects make it very hard for new rivals to catch up."
tm: More output, lower cost per unit.
y: "Network" literally means a net-like work of crossing threads, first used in the 1500s. The economic idea grew from studies of telephone networks.

h: That ₹20 chai customer is worth ₹20,000. Here's how. ☕
m: The total money one customer is likely to spend with you over their whole relationship.
e: A student who buys a Rs 20 chai every day for 3 years spends over Rs 20,000 at one stall.
i: "Knowing CLV tells us how much we can spend to win a new customer."
y: "Customer" comes from "custom", a habit: a customer is someone who habitually buys from you. From Latin consuetudo (habit).

h: You're rich on paper but can't pay for dinner. 🍽️
m: How quickly something can be turned into cash without losing value.
e: Money in your savings account is very liquid. A flat is not, because selling it can take months.
i: "Banks keep enough liquidity so customers can withdraw money any time."
y: From Latin liquidus (fluid, flowing). Liquid assets "flow" easily into cash.

h: The yearly meeting that decides your hike. 📈
m: A regular review of an employee's work, used for feedback, raises and promotions.
e: In March, a manager reviews the year's targets with each team member before salary hikes are decided.
i: "I would keep notes of my wins all year so my appraisal is backed by facts."
y: "Appraise" comes from Old French aprisier (to set a price on), from Latin pretium (price, value).

h: When a loan stops paying back, banks call it this. 🏦
m: A loan on which the borrower has not paid interest or the instalment for 90 days or more.
e: If a business stops paying its bank loan EMI for over three months, the bank marks that loan as an NPA.
i: "Rising NPAs hurt a bank's profits and its ability to lend."
tm: A loan being paid on time.
y: An acronym of Non-Performing Asset, the term used in Indian banking (as defined by the RBI) for a loan that has stopped earning interest or repayments.

h: Don't build the palace. Build the tent first. ⛺
m: The simplest version of a product that real customers can use, built to test the idea fast.
e: Before building an app, a student starts a WhatsApp group to sell notes. If people pay, the idea works.
i: "I would launch an MVP first and improve it with real customer feedback."
tm: A model, not for real users.
y: An acronym of Minimum Viable Product, a term coined by Frank Robinson around 2001 and made popular by Steve Blank and Eric Ries.

h: You don't buy this software. You rent it. 💻
m: Software you use online for a monthly or yearly fee, instead of buying and installing it.
e: Zoho, started in Chennai, sells online tools for email, accounts and HR to businesses on a subscription.
i: "SaaS companies like recurring revenue because customers keep paying every month."
y: An acronym of Software as a Service. "Software" was coined in the 1950s as the opposite of a computer's "hardware".

h: Not everyone is your customer. And that's okay. 🎯
m: Dividing a big market into smaller groups of people with similar needs.
e: A shoe brand makes one range for runners, one for office-goers and one for school kids.
i: "I would segment the market first, so each group gets a message that fits."
y: "Segment" comes from Latin segmentum (a piece cut off), from secare (to cut). The marketing idea was set out by Wendell Smith in 1956.

h: One page that shows what a company owns and owes 📄
m: A statement of a company's assets, liabilities and owners' equity on one date.
e: A company's balance sheet shows its factory and cash on one side, and its loans and owners' money on the other.
i: "I always read the balance sheet to check if a company has too much debt."
tm: Profit or loss over a period.
y: "Balance" comes from Latin bilanx, a scale with "two pans" (bi- + lanx): both sides must weigh the same.

h: Your work is judged by a number. Know yours 📏
m: A measurable number that shows how well a person or team is doing against a goal.
e: A customer support team's KPI could be 'solve 90% of complaints within 24 hours'.
i: "I like KPIs because they make expectations clear and fair."
y: An acronym of Key Performance Indicator. "Indicator" comes from Latin indicare (to point out).

h: Your bank can't lend all your money. Here's why 🏦
m: The share of deposits banks must keep with the RBI as cash, without earning interest.
e: If CRR is 4%, a bank with Rs 100 crore deposits must keep Rs 4 crore with the RBI.
i: "Raising CRR reduces money banks can lend, which can slow inflation."
y: An acronym of Cash Reserve Ratio. "Reserve" comes from Latin reservare (to keep back).

h: No investors. No loans. Just guts. 🚀
m: Building a business with your own savings and its own earnings, without outside investors.
e: Zerodha grew into one of India's biggest stock brokers without raising money from venture capital investors.
i: "We bootstrapped for the first year, so every rupee we spent had to earn its place."
y: From the phrase "pull yourself up by your bootstraps", the small loops at the back of a boot. It came to mean building something with only your own resources.

h: It's in your phone, your bank and your exams. AI 🤖
m: Computer systems that can do tasks that usually need human thinking, like understanding language.
e: Your phone's face unlock and a bank's fraud alert both use AI.
i: "I see AI as a tool that makes people more productive, not a replacement."
y: The term "artificial intelligence" was coined by John McCarthy for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop. "Intelligence" comes from Latin intelligere (to understand).

h: Talking to everyone means talking to no one. 📢
m: The specific group of people a product or ad is made for.
e: A coaching app for CAT aspirants targets graduates aged 21 to 26, not school students.
i: "Every campaign I plan starts with one question: who exactly is the target audience?"
wm: The people you want to reach.
y: "Target" comes from Old French targe, a small shield used for archery practice. "Audience" comes from Latin audire (to hear).

h: Did the company actually make money? This page tells 📈
m: A statement showing a company's income, expenses and profit over a period.
e: A company's yearly P&L shows Rs 100 crore sales, Rs 80 crore costs and Rs 20 crore profit.
i: "The P&L tells us if the business model is working."
y: "Profit" comes from Latin profectus (progress, advance). "Loss" comes from Old English los (destruction).

h: ₹6 LPA offer, but ₹38,000 in hand? Here's why 😅
m: The total yearly amount a company spends on an employee, including salary, PF and benefits.
e: A Rs 6 lakh CTC may include PF, insurance and bonus, so the monthly in-hand pay is lower.
i: "I always ask for the salary break-up, not just the CTC number."
wm: Total cost of you to the company.
y: An acronym of Cost to Company, a term used mainly in India for the full yearly cost of an employee to the employer.

h: Banks must keep some money 'safe'. By law 🔐
m: The share of deposits banks must keep in safe assets like government bonds, cash or gold.
e: A bank keeps part of its deposits in government securities to meet SLR rules.
i: "SLR makes sure banks can always meet sudden withdrawals."
y: An acronym of Statutory Liquidity Ratio. "Statutory" means set by statute (law), from Latin statuere (to set up).

h: The first stranger who believes in your idea 😇
m: A wealthy individual who invests their own money in a very early-stage startup.
e: A retired businessman puts Rs 25 lakh into two college friends' app idea for 10% equity.
i: "Angels bring money and advice when no bank will lend."
y: "Angel" was first used for wealthy backers of Broadway theatre shows in the early 1900s, later for early investors in startups.

h: How Netflix knows what you'll watch next 🎬
m: A type of AI where computers learn patterns from data instead of being told exact rules.
e: A video app learns from what you watch and suggests similar shows.
i: "Machine learning is only as good as the data it learns from."
y: The phrase "machine learning" was popularised by Arthur Samuel of IBM in 1959. "Machine" comes from Greek mekhane (device, contrivance).

h: Why does one brand feel 'premium' and another 'cheap'? 🤔
m: The place a brand wants to hold in the customer's mind compared with rivals.
e: Volvo is positioned on safety, while many car brands talk about mileage or style.
i: "Clear positioning helps customers remember why we are different."
wm: The image in the customer's mind.
tm: Name, logo and look of the brand.
y: The marketing sense was made famous by Al Ries and Jack Trout in the early 1970s: a brand's place in the customer's mind.

h: Profit on paper. Empty bank account. How? 💸
m: The actual money coming into and going out of a business.
e: A shop sells on credit and shows a profit, but has no cash because customers haven't paid yet.
i: "Cash flow is the oxygen of a business. Profit alone is not enough."
y: "Cash" comes from French caisse (money box), from Latin capsa (box).

h: The only salary number that pays your rent 🏠
m: The money that actually reaches your bank account after tax and deductions.
e: From a monthly gross of Rs 50,000, after PF and tax, the in-hand salary may be around Rs 44,000.
i: "When comparing offers, I compare in-hand salary, not just CTC."
y: "Salary" comes from Latin salarium, linked to sal (salt). It is often said Roman soldiers were paid in salt, though historians debate this.

h: How RBI controls prices without touching shop prices 🎛️
m: The RBI's actions on interest rates and money supply to control inflation and support growth.
e: RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meets every two months and decides whether to change the repo rate.
i: "Monetary policy works through banks, so its effects take months."
y: "Monetary" comes from Latin moneta, from the temple of Juno Moneta in Rome where coins were minted, the same root as "money".

h: They invest crores in startups that don't make profit yet 💼
m: Money from investment firms that fund fast-growing startups in exchange for equity.
e: A VC firm invests Rs 20 crore in a growing edtech startup for a 15% stake.
i: "VCs expect big growth, so they push startups to scale quickly."
y: "Venture" is short for "adventure", from Latin advenire (to arrive, happen): a risky undertaking.

h: AI that writes, draws and composes. What now? ✨
m: AI that creates new content like text, images, music or code.
e: Students use AI chat tools to explain hard topics, and designers use AI to draft images.
i: "Generative AI is powerful, but its answers must always be checked."
y: "Generative" comes from Latin generare (to produce, beget). The phrase spread widely after 2022 with tools like ChatGPT.

h: Every product launch rests on just 4 letters. 🧩
m: The four choices every marketer makes: product, price, place and promotion.
e: A new biscuit brand decides its taste, sets a Rs 10 pack, sells in kirana shops and runs TV ads.
i: "I would review all 4Ps together, because changing one affects the others."
y: The phrase "marketing mix" was coined by Neil Borden of Harvard in the late 1940s. E. Jerome McCarthy grouped it into the 4Ps in 1960.

h: A ₹100 shirt. How much is real profit? 👕
m: Sales minus the direct cost of making the product, shown as a percentage.
e: A shirt sells for Rs 1,000 and costs Rs 400 to make. Gross margin is 60%.
i: "Higher gross margin gives a business more room to spend on growth."
y: "Margin" comes from Latin margo (edge, border): the gap between what you sell for and what it costs.

h: Got a new job? You can't leave tomorrow ⏳
m: The time an employee must keep working after resigning, before they can leave.
e: Many Indian IT companies have a 60 to 90 day notice period.
i: "I would serve my notice period properly to leave on good terms."
y: "Notice" comes from Latin notitia (knowledge, being known), from noscere (to get to know).

h: The government's two big levers: tax and spending 🏛️
m: The government's decisions on taxes and spending to guide the economy.
e: Building more highways to create jobs during a slowdown is fiscal policy.
i: "Fiscal policy can boost demand quickly, but adds to borrowing."
y: "Fiscal" comes from Latin fiscus, the basket used to hold the Roman state's tax money. "Policy" comes from Greek polis (city, state).

h: New year, new goals. Here's how top companies set them 🎯
m: A goal-setting method: one clear objective plus 3 to 5 measurable results.
e: Objective: grow Instagram. Key results: 10,000 followers, 5% engagement, 3 reels a week.
i: "OKRs keep everyone focused on the few goals that matter most."

h: Every swipe you make is data. Lots of it 📊
m: Extremely large sets of data that need special tools to store and study.
e: An e-commerce site studies crores of clicks daily to know what people want.
i: "Big data helps companies decide with facts instead of guesses."
tm: Data a person can analyse by hand.

h: Every product is born, grows old and fades. Even yours. 📉
m: The stages a product goes through: launch, growth, maturity and decline.
e: Feature phones grew fast, matured, and declined once smartphones arrived.
i: "Knowing the life-cycle stage tells us whether to invest more or plan a new product."

h: Out of every ₹100 earned, what's really left? 💰
m: Net profit as a percentage of total sales, after all costs and taxes.
e: A company with Rs 100 crore sales and Rs 8 crore net profit has an 8% net margin.
i: "Net margin shows how much of each rupee of sales the company keeps."

h: Your first 6 months are a trial. For both sides 🧪
m: A trial period after joining, when the company checks if the employee is a good fit.
e: A fresher joins with a 6-month probation, after which the job is confirmed.
i: "I treat probation as my chance to prove my value quickly."

h: Is your monthly kharcha going up? This number knows 🛒
m: An index that tracks changes in prices of everyday goods and services that households buy.
e: CPI tracks prices of things like rice, milk, vegetables, rent and fuel.
i: "RBI watches CPI inflation closely when setting interest rates."

h: Every big tree starts as a seed. Startups too 🌱
m: The first money raised to turn an idea into a working product.
e: Founders raise Rs 50 lakh of seed money to build their first app and hire 3 people.
i: "Seed funding is about proving the idea works."

h: Turning numbers into decisions. Every company needs it 📈
m: Studying data to find patterns and make better business decisions.
e: A retail chain finds that umbrellas sell more in July, so it stocks up in June.
i: "Analytics turns raw data into clear actions."

h: Why new apps give you things almost free at first 🎁
m: Launching at a very low price to win customers quickly, then raising it later.
e: A new telecom operator gave free data for months to win millions of users fast.
i: "Penetration pricing works when the market is price-sensitive and growing."

h: The day your business stops losing money 🎯
m: The level of sales where total income equals total costs, so there is no profit or loss.
e: A café with Rs 1 lakh monthly costs and Rs 100 profit per cup breaks even at 1,000 cups.
i: "Knowing the break-even point tells us how much we must sell to survive."

h: Read these 5 lines before you sign anything ✍️
m: A formal letter from a company offering you a job, with role, salary and joining date.
e: Riya's offer letter lists her role, CTC, joining date, location and notice period.
i: "I read the whole offer letter, especially bond and notice clauses, before accepting."

h: Prices rise in factories first. Then in shops 🏭
m: An index that tracks price changes of goods sold in bulk by producers and wholesalers.
e: WPI tracks prices of things like steel, fuel and grains at the wholesale level.
i: "WPI often signals future changes in retail prices."

h: 'We raised our Series A!' What does that mean? 🅰️
m: The first major round of venture funding, after a startup shows early traction.
e: A startup with 1 lakh users raises Rs 40 crore in Series A to expand to new cities.
i: "Series A investors look for a clear path to growth."

h: Your photos aren't 'in the sky'. Here's where they are ☁️
m: Using storage and computing power over the internet instead of your own computers.
e: A startup rents servers online and pays only for what it uses, instead of buying machines.
i: "The cloud lets small companies use big-company technology."

h: Why new phones cost more on launch day 📱
m: Starting with a high price for early buyers, then lowering it over time.
e: A new flagship phone launches at a high price, then gets cheaper a few months later.
i: "Skimming suits products that early fans will pay extra for."
tm: Low price first to win share.

h: Sell 0 or sell 1,000. You still pay this 🏢
m: A cost that stays the same no matter how much you sell, like rent.
e: A coaching centre pays Rs 50,000 rent whether it has 10 students or 100.
i: "High fixed costs make a business risky when sales drop."

h: Yes, they will call your old college. And old boss 📞
m: Checking a candidate's education, past jobs and records before or after hiring.
e: A company verifies your degree with the university and calls your previous employer.
i: "Honest CVs make background checks a formality."
tm: Talking to people who know you.

h: Every economy fears this word. Here's what it means 📉
m: A period when an economy shrinks, with falling output, jobs and incomes.
e: During a recession, companies hire less, sales fall and people spend carefully.
i: "In a recession, I would focus on cost control and essential products."

h: A startup worth $1 billion. India has over 100 🦄
m: A privately held startup valued at more than one billion US dollars.
e: India has produced well over a hundred unicorns in fintech, edtech and e-commerce.
i: "A unicorn valuation is impressive, but profit matters in the long run."

h: One weak password can sink a whole company 🔐
m: Protecting computers, networks and data from attacks and theft.
e: Banks use two-factor login and monitoring to stop hackers stealing customer money.
i: "Cybersecurity is everyone's job, not just the IT team's."

h: Why is it always ₹99 and never ₹100? 🧠
m: Setting prices that feel cheaper to the mind, like Rs 99 instead of Rs 100.
e: A T-shirt priced at Rs 499 feels much cheaper than one priced at Rs 500.
i: "Small pricing tricks can lift sales without changing the product."

h: Sell more, spend more. Naturally 📦
m: A cost that rises or falls with the amount you produce or sell.
e: A pizza shop spends more on cheese and dough when it sells more pizzas.
i: "Lower variable cost per unit improves profit as we scale."

h: The most honest talk you'll have with HR 🚪
m: A conversation with an employee who is leaving, to learn why they are leaving.
e: HR asks a leaving employee what they liked, what they didn't and why they are going.
i: "Exit interviews show patterns that help reduce attrition."
tm: Talk to keep people from leaving.

h: Prices rising AND no growth? Worst of both 😬
m: When an economy has high inflation, slow growth and high unemployment together.
e: Prices of fuel and food rise sharply while jobs and growth stay weak.
i: "Stagflation is hard to fix, because raising rates slows growth further."
tm: Prices rising, growth may be fine.

h: Almost a unicorn. Just not yet 🐴
m: A startup expected to reach a $1 billion valuation soon.
e: A fast-growing logistics startup valued at $600 million is called a soonicorn.
i: "Soonicorns attract investor attention and top talent."

h: 'Your account is blocked. Click here.' Don't! 🎣
m: Fake messages or websites that trick people into sharing passwords or bank details.
e: A fake SMS says 'Your KYC is pending, click this link', and steals your bank login.
i: "I never click links in unknown messages and always check the sender."

h: Today the whole country checks one speech. Why? 📜
m: The central government's yearly plan of income and spending, presented on 1 February.
e: The Finance Minister announces tax changes, new schemes and spending plans in Parliament.
i: "I read the budget to see which sectors the government is backing."
tm: Report on the economy before the budget.

h: Your new bike loses value every year. So do machines 🏍️
m: The fall in value of an asset over time because of use and age.
e: A company buys a Rs 10 lakh machine and records Rs 1 lakh as depreciation each year for 10 years.
i: "Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset over the years it is used."

h: Why some companies get 10,000 applications for 1 job ⭐
m: How a company is seen as a place to work.
e: Companies post team photos, learning stories and employee reviews to look like a great workplace.
i: "Strong employer branding attracts better talent at lower hiring cost."

h: India buys more from the world than it sells. Is that bad? 🌍
m: When a country spends more on imports and payments abroad than it earns from exports and income.
e: India imports a lot of oil and gold, which adds to its current account deficit.
i: "A small CAD is normal for a growing country, but a big one is risky."
tm: Imports more than exports of goods.

h: Before the money, comes this document 📝
m: A short document listing the main terms of an investment before the final deal.
e: A term sheet says the investor will put Rs 5 crore for 20% equity and get a board seat.
i: "I would read every clause of a term sheet with a lawyer."

h: A record book that nobody can secretly change ⛓️
m: A shared digital record where entries are linked and very hard to alter.
e: Some companies use blockchain to track food supply from farm to shop.
i: "Blockchain is useful where many parties need one trusted record."

h: Burger alone or the meal? You know what you picked 🍔
m: Selling two or more products together at one price.
e: Fast-food chains sell a burger, fries and a drink as one meal that costs less than buying each.
i: "Bundling raises the average bill while giving customers better value."

h: Not everything you own is an asset. Really 🏠
m: Things a business or person owns that have value, like cash, buildings or machines.
e: A bakery's assets include its ovens, delivery van, stock of flour and cash in the bank.
i: "I look at whether assets are earning money or just sitting idle."

h: Your job is part of life. Not all of it ⚖️
m: Managing time so that work does not take over family, health and rest.
e: A company with fixed logout times and no weekend emails supports work-life balance.
i: "Good balance keeps people productive for the long run."
wm: Healthy split of work and life.

h: India's emergency piggy bank, in dollars 💵
m: Foreign currencies and gold held by the RBI to pay for imports and protect the rupee.
e: The RBI can sell dollars from its reserves when the rupee falls too fast.
i: "Strong forex reserves give confidence to foreign investors."
tm: Gold held by the central bank.

h: You raised money. Your share just got smaller 🥧
m: The drop in a founder's ownership percentage when new shares are issued to investors.
e: A founder owns 100%, raises funding for 20%, and now owns 80%.
i: "Some dilution is fine if the company's value grows faster."

h: Digital money with no bank. Risky or the future? 🪙
m: Digital currency that runs on blockchain and is not issued by any government.
e: Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, and its price can rise or fall sharply in days.
i: "Crypto is highly risky, so I would never invest money I can't afford to lose."

h: 'Want a case with that phone?' There's a word for it 📲
m: Suggesting a related product to a customer who is already buying.
e: An online store shows phone covers and screen guards when you add a phone to your cart.
i: "Cross-selling increases revenue from customers we already have."

h: That loan isn't money you have. It's money you owe 📋
m: Money a business or person owes to others, like loans or unpaid bills.
e: A shop's liabilities include its bank loan and money owed to suppliers.
i: "Too many liabilities compared with assets is a warning sign."

h: Tired even after sleeping 9 hours? Read this 🔋
m: A state of physical and mental exhaustion caused by long-term stress at work or study.
e: A student studying 14 hours daily for months starts feeling empty and loses all motivation.
i: "Preventing burnout needs breaks, boundaries and support."

h: Why your US college fees went up without any hike ✈️
m: When the rupee loses value against other currencies like the dollar.
e: If $1 goes from Rs 80 to Rs 85, imported phones and foreign fees get costlier.
i: "A weaker rupee helps exporters but hurts importers."

h: Who owns how much of the startup? One sheet shows 📊
m: A table showing who owns what percentage of a company.
e: A cap table lists: Founder A 40%, Founder B 30%, investors 25%, ESOP pool 5%.
i: "A clean cap table makes future fundraising easier."

h: Your fridge can talk to your phone now 📡
m: Everyday devices connected to the internet so they can send and receive data.
e: A smart meter sends electricity usage to the power company automatically.
i: "IoT helps businesses track machines and save energy."

h: From medium to large in one smile. Smart move. 🥤
m: Encouraging a customer to buy a better or more expensive version.
e: A cinema counter asks if you want a large popcorn for just Rs 40 more.
i: "Upselling works when the upgrade genuinely gives more value."

h: Who really owns the company? Equity holders 🧾
m: The owners' share in a business: assets minus liabilities.
e: If a shop has Rs 10 lakh assets and Rs 4 lakh loans, the owner's equity is Rs 6 lakh.
i: "Founders give up some equity when investors put money in."

h: Doing only what the job description says. Is it wrong? 🤫
m: Doing only the minimum work required, without extra effort.
e: An employee logs in and out on time, does assigned tasks, but stops volunteering for anything more.
i: "Quiet quitting is often a sign of poor engagement, not laziness."

h: How many rupees for one dollar? It changes daily 💱
m: The price of one country's currency in terms of another.
e: If $1 = Rs 84, a $100 online course costs about Rs 8,400.
i: "Exchange rates affect everything from oil prices to IT company profits."
wm: Price of one currency in another.

h: Investors always ask: how do we get our money back? 🚪
m: A plan for how founders and investors will eventually sell their stake.
e: Investors expect an exit through an IPO or the company being bought by a bigger firm.
i: "A clear exit strategy makes investors more comfortable."

h: The robot didn't take your job. It took your boring tasks 🤖
m: Using machines or software to do tasks without human effort.
e: A bank uses software to send automatic EMI reminders instead of staff calling.
i: "Automation frees people to focus on work that needs judgement."

h: You'll walk to 3 shops for your favourite brand. Why? ❤️
m: When customers keep choosing the same brand again and again.
e: Many families have bought the same toothpaste brand for years without trying others.
i: "Brand loyalty lowers marketing cost because loyal customers return on their own."

h: Is the company running on loans? This ratio knows ⚖️
m: Total debt divided by owners' equity. It shows how much a business depends on loans.
e: A company with Rs 50 crore debt and Rs 100 crore equity has a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.5.
i: "A very high ratio means the company carries a lot of risk."

h: Day job + night job. Allowed or not? 🌙
m: Doing a second job secretly or alongside a main full-time job.
e: An IT engineer works for his company by day and freelances for another firm at night.
i: "Moonlighting rules depend on your contract, so always check it."
wm: A second job on the side.
tm: Your own small business on the side.

h: Why global companies build factories in India 🏭
m: When a foreign company invests directly in a business or factory in another country.
e: A global phone maker sets up a factory in Tamil Nadu. That's FDI.
i: "FDI brings jobs, technology and long-term capital."
tm: Foreign money in shares and bonds.

h: When a big company buys a startup whole 🛒
m: When one company buys another company and takes control of it.
e: A food delivery app acquired a quick-commerce startup to enter grocery delivery.
i: "Acquisitions help big firms grow fast, but merging cultures is hard."

h: One software that runs an entire company 🏭
m: Software that connects a company's finance, HR, inventory and sales in one system.
e: A factory uses ERP so sales, stock and accounts update together automatically.
i: "ERP gives managers one clear view of the whole business."
wm: One system for the whole firm.

h: Same work. Different pay. Still? ⚖️
m: The difference in average pay between men and women.
e: Studies show women in many sectors earn less than men for similar roles.
i: "Fair pay audits help companies close the gender pay gap."

h: Some shares pay you just for holding them 💵
m: A part of a company's profit paid to its shareholders.
e: A company declares a Rs 10 dividend per share, so someone with 100 shares gets Rs 1,000.
i: "Steady dividends often show a mature, profitable business."

h: 3 days office, 2 days home. The new normal? 🏠🏢
m: A work model that mixes working from the office and from home.
e: A bank lets its staff work from office on Monday to Wednesday and from home on Thursday and Friday.
i: "Hybrid work needs clear goals and good communication."

h: Foreign money that can leave India in one click 💻
m: When foreign investors buy shares or bonds of a country without controlling companies.
e: A US fund buys shares of Indian banks on the stock market. That's FPI.
i: "FPI money is fast-moving, so markets swing when it leaves."
tm: Foreign money in factories and firms.

h: How many months before your startup runs out of cash? ✈️
m: The number of months a startup can survive with the cash it has.
e: With Rs 60 lakh in the bank and Rs 5 lakh burn a month, the runway is 12 months.
i: "Founders should start fundraising at least 6 months before runway ends."

h: How companies remember every customer's birthday 🎂
m: Software and processes to manage customer data and relationships.
e: A car dealer's CRM reminds the team to call customers when their service is due.
i: "A good CRM turns one-time buyers into loyal customers."

h: Why do cricketers sell everything from bikes to biscuits? 🏏
m: A well-known person who represents a brand and promotes it.
e: Sports stars and film actors often appear in ads as the face of a brand.
i: "A good ambassador shares the brand's values, not just fame."

h: How a private company lets you become its owner 🔔
m: When a company sells its shares to the public for the first time.
e: When a popular food delivery company listed on the stock market, lakhs of people applied in its IPO.
i: "An IPO raises money for growth and lets early investors sell some shares."
wm: Company's first public sale of shares.

h: The skill that got you hired won't keep you hired 📚
m: Learning new skills to do your current job better.
e: An accountant learns advanced Excel and data tools to work faster.
i: "I upskill every year, because tools keep changing."

h: When the government sells its share in a company 🏷️
m: The government selling part or all of its stake in public sector companies.
e: The government sold its stake in Air India to the Tata group.
i: "Disinvestment raises money and can make companies more efficient."

h: The moment customers start pulling your product 🧲
m: When a product meets a real market need so well that customers keep buying and recommending it.
e: An app's users grow by word of mouth, and most of them use it daily without ads.
i: "Before scaling, I would make sure we have product-market fit."

h: How apps talk to each other behind the scenes 🔌
m: A set of rules that lets one software use the features or data of another.
e: A food app shows maps by using a map company's API.
i: "APIs let companies build faster by connecting existing services."

h: Why food brands love red and banks love blue 🎨
m: How colours affect how people feel about a brand or product.
e: Many food chains use red and yellow because they feel energetic and appetising.
i: "Colour choices shape first impressions before a word is read."
tm: The full look of a brand.

h: How the market decides what a company is worth 🏦
m: The total value of a company's shares: share price times number of shares.
e: A company with 10 crore shares at Rs 500 each has a market cap of Rs 5,000 crore.
i: "Market cap tells us size, but not whether the share is cheap or expensive."

h: Your job may change. You can change faster 🔄
m: Learning new skills to move into a different role.
e: A call centre employee learns data analysis and moves into an analytics team.
i: "Reskilling helps people stay employed as technology changes jobs."

h: Owned by the government, listed on the stock market 🏢
m: A company in which the government holds the majority stake.
e: SBI, ONGC and Coal India are well-known PSUs.
i: "PSUs often have stable dividends but slower decision-making."

h: 10 slides that decide crores. No pressure 😅
m: A short presentation founders use to explain their startup to investors.
e: A deck covers the problem, solution, market size, business model, team and the ask.
i: "A great pitch deck tells a story, not just numbers."

h: Why your feed shows THAT reel first 📲
m: A set of step-by-step instructions a computer follows to solve a problem.
e: Instagram's algorithm decides which posts you see first based on what you engage with.
i: "Understanding algorithms helps creators and brands reach more people."

h: You trust a creator more than an ad. Brands know it. 📸
m: Brands working with social media creators to promote products to their followers.
e: A skincare brand sends products to beauty creators who review them on Instagram.
i: "I would pick influencers whose followers match our target audience, not just big numbers."
tm: Film or sports stars in ads.

h: 'Sensex up 500 points.' What does that even mean? 📈
m: An index of 30 large companies on the Bombay Stock Exchange that shows how the market is moving.
e: When the news says Sensex rose 1%, it means these 30 big companies' shares went up on average.
i: "The Sensex is a quick mood check of India's stock market."

h: What happens when the boss leaves tomorrow? 👑
m: Preparing people inside a company to take over key roles in future.
e: A company trains two managers so one can become the next sales head.
i: "Succession planning keeps a company stable during leadership changes."

h: Why companies celebrate New Year on 1 April 📅
m: The 12-month period used for accounts and taxes. In India it runs from 1 April to 31 March.
e: FY 2027-28 starts on 1 April 2027 and ends on 31 March 2028.
i: "Companies plan budgets and targets around the financial year."

h: Explain your idea in 30 seconds. Go! ⏱️
m: A very short, clear explanation of an idea or yourself, short enough for a lift ride.
e: 'We help small kirana shops order stock on WhatsApp in 2 minutes.'
i: "I practise a 30-second pitch for interviews and networking."

h: Old business, new tech. Adapt or disappear 🔄
m: Using digital technology to change how a business works and serves customers.
e: A traditional bank moves account opening, loans and support to a mobile app.
i: "Digital transformation is about changing processes, not just buying software."

h: Give value first. Sell later. It works. ✍️
m: Attracting customers by sharing useful content instead of direct ads.
e: A home loan company posts free videos on how to plan your first house purchase.
i: "Content marketing builds trust, so customers come to us when they are ready to buy."

h: 50 companies that show India's market mood 🇮🇳
m: An index of 50 large companies on the National Stock Exchange.
e: Many index funds simply buy all 50 Nifty companies in the same proportion.
i: "Tracking the Nifty is an easy way to see the overall market trend."

h: Recruiting fills seats. This builds teams 🎯
m: The long-term process of finding, attracting and hiring the right people.
e: A company builds relationships with colleges to hire good graduates every year.
i: "Talent acquisition thinks about future needs, not just today's opening."

h: That cheap LPG cylinder? Someone paid the rest 🔥
m: Money the government pays to lower the price of something for people or businesses.
e: The government gives a subsidy on fertilisers so farmers can buy them cheaply.
i: "Subsidies help the needy, but must be targeted to avoid waste."
wm: Government paying part of the cost.

h: Great idea. But how does it make money? 💡
m: The plan for how a business creates value and earns money.
e: A food app earns commission from restaurants and delivery fees from customers.
i: "Investors care about the business model as much as the idea."

h: From 'go to market' to 'market comes to you' 🛒
m: Buying and selling goods or services over the internet.
e: People in small towns now order clothes and electronics online and get them in a few days.
i: "E-commerce lets small sellers reach customers across India."

h: Page 2 of Google is where websites go to hide 🔍
m: Improving a website so it shows up higher in search results.
e: A Jaipur bakery adds 'best cakes in Jaipur' to its site so local searchers find it.
i: "Good SEO brings free, steady traffic from people already looking for us."

h: Don't know which share to buy? Let experts pick 🧺
m: A pool of money from many investors, managed by a professional who invests it.
e: Thousands of people put money in a fund, and the fund manager invests it in many companies.
i: "Mutual funds give small investors diversification and expert management."

h: Baisakhi means harvest. Harvest means this word 🌾
m: The minimum price at which the government promises to buy certain crops from farmers.
e: The government announces MSP for wheat before the harvest, so farmers know their minimum price.
i: "MSP protects farmers from sudden price crashes."
tm: Price set by buyers and sellers.

h: Why 'Made in India' is now on so many phones 📱
m: A government campaign launched in 2014 to make India a manufacturing hub.
e: Many global brands now assemble phones and electronics in Indian factories.
i: "Make in India aims to create jobs and cut dependence on imports."

h: Ads, subscriptions or commission? Pick one 💳
m: The specific way a business earns money from customers.
e: A news app may earn through ads, a monthly subscription, or both.
i: "Choosing the right revenue model decides how fast we can grow."

h: What UPI did for payments, this wants to do for shopping 🛍️
m: A government-backed open network that lets buyers and sellers trade across different apps.
e: A seller listed on one app can be discovered by buyers using a different app.
i: "ONDC could help small sellers reach customers without big platform fees."

h: 'Buy now'. 'Sign up'. 'Swipe up'. Why every ad ends this way 👆
m: A clear line that tells people exactly what to do next.
e: A sale banner ends with 'Shop now, offer ends tonight'.
i: "Every ad needs one clear call to action, or people just scroll past."
wm: Telling people what to do next.

h: ₹500 a month can grow big. Here's the trick 🌱
m: Investing a fixed amount in a mutual fund every month, automatically.
e: Aman invests Rs 1,000 every month through a SIP from his first salary.
i: "SIP builds discipline and averages out market ups and downs."

h: Your first job might come to your college. Be ready 🎓
m: When companies visit colleges to hire final-year students.
e: Companies conduct tests, group discussions and interviews on campus in the final year.
i: "Campus placements reward students who prepare early."

h: The government pays companies to make more in India 💡
m: A scheme that gives companies cash rewards for increasing production in India.
e: Phone makers get incentives for every extra phone they produce in India above a target.
i: "PLI links support to real output, not just promises."

h: Losing money on every order? Scaling won't fix it 🧮
m: The profit or loss a business makes on a single unit, like one order or one customer.
e: If a delivery costs Rs 60 and earns Rs 50, the startup loses Rs 10 per order.
i: "Positive unit economics must come before rapid scaling."

h: The Indian invention the whole world is copying 🇮🇳
m: India's instant system for sending money between bank accounts using a phone.
e: You scan a QR code at a tea stall and pay Rs 20 in two seconds.
i: "UPI made digital payments simple for crores of Indians."

h: 1,000 visitors. 20 buyers. That number matters most 📊
m: The percentage of visitors who take the action you want, like buying.
e: If 1,000 people visit an online shop and 20 buy, the conversion rate is 2%.
i: "I would improve conversion rate before spending more money on traffic."

h: Einstein reportedly called it a wonder. Here's why ✨
m: Interest earned on your money and also on the interest already earned.
e: Rs 1 lakh at 10% becomes Rs 1.1 lakh in a year, then Rs 1.21 lakh the next, and keeps growing faster.
i: "Starting early matters most, because compounding needs time."
tm: Interest only on the original sum.

h: What if your salary came with a piece of the company? 📜
m: A plan that gives employees the right to own company shares, usually after some years.
e: A startup gives early employees ESOPs, which became valuable when the company grew.
i: "ESOPs reward employees who help a company grow over time."

h: India's biggest advantage? Its young people 🧑‍🎓
m: The economic boost a country gets when it has many working-age people compared with dependents.
e: India has one of the world's largest young populations, ready to work and spend.
i: "The dividend pays off only if young people get skills and jobs."

h: Can your business serve 1 crore customers? 📈
m: The ability of a business to grow fast without costs growing at the same speed.
e: An app can add lakhs of users with little extra cost, but a salon needs new chairs and staff.
i: "Investors love scalable models because profits grow faster than costs."

h: Aadhaar + UPI + DigiLocker = digital India 🧱
m: A set of digital public systems like Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker that services can build on.
e: Opening a bank account with Aadhaar e-KYC in minutes uses India Stack.
i: "India Stack shows how public tech can serve a billion people."

h: Red button or green button? Don't guess. Test. 🔬
m: Showing two versions to different people to see which works better.
e: An app shows half its users a red 'Buy' button and half a green one, then keeps the winner.
i: "A/B testing lets data, not opinions, decide."

h: Never put all your eggs in one basket 🧺
m: Spreading money across different investments to reduce risk.
e: Instead of all savings in one share, Neha invests in a fund, a fixed deposit and some gold.
i: "Diversification protects you when one investment does badly."

h: The part of your salary that depends on you 🎯
m: Pay that changes with performance, like bonus or incentives.
e: A sales executive gets a fixed salary plus incentives based on monthly sales.
i: "Variable pay links rewards directly to results."

h: Degrees rising. Jobs? Here's the number 📊
m: The percentage of people who want to work and are looking, but cannot find a job.
e: If 100 people are looking for work and 8 can't find jobs, unemployment is 8%.
i: "I watch unemployment data to understand the real health of an economy."

h: A nursery for baby startups 🐣
m: An organisation that supports very early startups with space, mentors and resources.
e: Many IITs and IIMs run incubators where student startups get office space and guidance.
i: "Incubators help founders avoid common early mistakes."

h: See the sofa in your room before you buy it 🛋️
m: Technology that adds digital images on top of the real world through a phone or glasses.
e: A furniture app lets you place a virtual sofa in your living room using the camera.
i: "AR helps customers buy with more confidence online."

h: Why 100 people see your ad but only 2 buy 🌪️
m: The journey from first hearing about a product to finally buying it.
e: 1,000 see an ad, 200 visit the site, 50 add to cart and 10 buy. Each step is a funnel stage.
i: "I would find the stage where most people drop out and fix that first."

h: When everyone suddenly becomes a stock expert 🐂
m: A period when share prices are rising and investors feel confident.
e: In a bull market, the Sensex keeps making new highs and more people open demat accounts.
i: "Bull markets reward patience, but they can also make people careless."

h: Stay 5 years and get a thank-you cheque 🎁
m: A lump sum paid by an employer to an employee after about 5 years of continuous service.
e: An employee leaving after 6 years gets gratuity based on his last salary and years worked.
i: "Gratuity is a reward for loyalty and long service."

h: India's GDP is huge. So why do many feel poor? 🤔
m: A country's total income divided by its population.
e: A big GDP shared among 140 crore people gives a much smaller amount per person.
i: "Per capita income shows living standards better than total GDP."

h: 3 months that can change a startup's life ⚡
m: A short, intense program that helps startups grow fast, often for a small equity stake.
e: A startup joins a 3-month accelerator, gets mentorship and pitches to investors on demo day.
i: "Accelerators speed up learning, networking and fundraising."

h: Faster than 4G. But that's not the big change 📶
m: The fifth generation of mobile networks, with much higher speed and lower delay.
e: 5G can support remote surgery and smart factories that need instant connections.
i: "5G will matter most for industries, not just faster videos."

h: Every 'free webinar' you sign up for has a purpose 🧲
m: Collecting contact details of people who may become customers.
e: An MBA college offers a free career guide in exchange for your name and phone number.
i: "Good lead generation brings in people who actually need the product."

h: Prices falling. Panic rising. Don't run 🐻
m: A period when share prices fall a lot and investors feel worried.
e: During a bear market, share prices may fall 20% or more from their highs.
i: "Bear markets test patience, and long-term investors often buy then."

h: That PF cut every month? It's your future money 🏦
m: A retirement savings scheme where both employee and employer put in a share of salary every month.
e: 12% of basic salary goes to EPF from the employee, and the employer adds a share too.
i: "PF is forced saving that builds a solid retirement fund."

h: Why onions suddenly cost ₹100 🧅
m: The basic rule that prices rise when demand is more than supply, and fall when supply is more.
e: When heavy rain damages onion crops, supply falls and onion prices shoot up.
i: "Almost every price change can be explained by supply and demand."

h: The government scheme every founder should know 🇮🇳
m: A government initiative launched in 2016 that gives recognised startups tax benefits, easier rules and funding support.
e: A DPIIT-recognised startup can get tax benefits and easier compliance.
i: "I would register with Startup India to use its benefits early."

h: The tiny chip that runs your entire life 💾
m: Materials used to make chips that power phones, cars and computers.
e: A modern car has hundreds of chips, and a chip shortage once stopped car factories worldwide.
i: "India is building chip factories to reduce dependence on imports."

h: What does it cost to win one customer? Most guess wrong 💰
m: The total marketing and sales money spent to win one new customer.
e: If a startup spends Rs 1 lakh on ads and gets 500 customers, its CAC is Rs 200.
i: "A business is healthy when customer lifetime value is much higher than CAC."

h: Is that share cheap or expensive? One number helps 🔢
m: A company's share price divided by its earnings per share.
e: A share at Rs 200 with Rs 10 earnings per share has a P/E of 20.
i: "A high P/E means investors expect strong future growth."

h: Happy employees work better. Engaged ones work best 💪
m: How involved and committed employees feel towards their work and company.
e: Engaged employees suggest ideas, help teammates and care about results.
i: "Engagement improves when people feel valued and see growth."

h: The real price of a choice is what you give up ⏳
m: The value of the best option you give up when you choose something else.
e: Spending 3 hours on reels has an opportunity cost: 3 hours you could have studied.
i: "I think about opportunity cost before every big decision."

h: Choosing a co-founder is like choosing a life partner 🤝
m: One of the people who start a company together and share ownership.
e: One co-founder handles tech while the other handles sales and fundraising.
i: "Co-founders with different skills but shared values build stronger startups."

h: Petrol pumps or charging points? The road ahead 🔋
m: A vehicle that runs on electricity stored in batteries instead of petrol or diesel.
e: Electric scooters and e-rickshaws are now common on Indian roads.
i: "EV growth depends on cheaper batteries and more charging points."

h: Customers leaving quietly? There's a number for that 🚪
m: The percentage of customers who stop using a product in a given period.
e: If 100 of 1,000 subscribers cancel a streaming plan in a month, churn is 10%.
i: "Reducing churn is often cheaper than finding new customers."

h: How much profit does each share earn? 🧮
m: A company's net profit divided by the number of shares.
e: A company with Rs 100 crore profit and 10 crore shares has EPS of Rs 10.
i: "Rising EPS over years is a good sign of a growing company."

h: Your boss, peers and juniors all review you 🔄
m: Feedback about an employee from managers, colleagues, juniors and sometimes clients.
e: A team leader gets anonymous feedback from her manager, 5 peers and her team.
i: "360 feedback gives a fuller picture than one manager's view."

h: Petrol up, people still buy. Chips up? Not so much ⛽
m: How much demand changes when the price changes.
e: If chips cost more, people buy less. Salt sales barely change even if its price rises.
i: "Knowing elasticity helps decide how far a price can be raised."

h: Why founders don't get all their shares on day one ⏳
m: Earning your shares slowly over time, usually 4 years, instead of all at once.
e: An employee's ESOPs vest 25% each year over 4 years.
i: "Vesting keeps founders and employees committed for the long run."

h: Investors now ask: are you good for the planet? 🌍
m: A way to judge companies on their care for environment, people and honest management.
e: Funds check a company's pollution, worker safety and board honesty before investing.
i: "Strong ESG practices can lower risk and attract investors."

h: One question decides how much customers love you ⭐
m: A score based on how likely customers are to recommend you to a friend.
e: After a cab ride, the app asks: 'How likely are you to recommend us, 0 to 10?'
i: "I would track NPS monthly to spot unhappy customers early."

h: A 3-digit number that decides your loans 💳
m: A score that shows how reliably you have repaid loans and credit card bills.
e: A good CIBIL score, say above 750, helps you get a loan faster and at a lower rate.
i: "I would protect my credit score by paying every EMI and card bill on time."
tm: Most you can borrow on a card.

h: Why only a few in a team get top ratings 🔔
m: A rating method where most employees get average ratings and only a few get top or bottom ones.
e: In a team of 10, maybe 2 get 'excellent', 6 'good' and 2 'needs improvement'.
i: "Bell curves can feel unfair in small, high-performing teams."

h: One seller, no choice. That's power 👑
m: A market where only one company sells a product with no close substitute.
e: Indian Railways is the only company running train services across most of India.
i: "Monopolies can charge high prices, so they are often regulated."

h: Build. Measure. Learn. Repeat. 🔁
m: A method of building a startup by testing small ideas quickly and learning from customers.
e: Founders test a simple landing page first to see if people sign up, before building the app.
i: "The lean approach saves money by learning before building big."

h: Your daily coffee has a climate cost ☕
m: The total greenhouse gases caused by a person, product or company.
e: A flight from Delhi to Mumbai has a much bigger carbon footprint than the same trip by train.
i: "Measuring carbon footprint is the first step to reducing it."

h: The cheapest ad in the world is a happy customer 🗣️
m: When customers tell others about a product on their own.
e: A small momo stall becomes famous in a city because students keep telling friends about it.
i: "Great service creates word of mouth that no ad budget can buy."

h: That 'easy EMI' isn't always easy 📅
m: A fixed amount paid every month to repay a loan with interest.
e: A Rs 60,000 phone on a 12-month EMI means paying around Rs 5,000-plus every month.
i: "Before taking an EMI, I check the total interest, not just the monthly amount."

h: One good mentor can save you 5 years of mistakes 🧭
m: A relationship where an experienced person guides someone less experienced.
e: A senior manager meets a new joinee every month to guide her career choices.
i: "I look for mentors who tell me honest truths, not just nice words."

h: Why only 3-4 telecom companies serve 140 crore people 📶
m: A market controlled by a few large companies.
e: India's mobile network market is led by a few big telecom operators.
i: "In an oligopoly, one company's price move quickly affects others."

h: How a new idea kills an old industry 💥
m: When a new product or business model replaces an established way of doing things.
e: Digital payments disrupted the need to carry cash for small purchases.
i: "Disruptors win by making things simpler, cheaper or faster."

h: Use, reuse, recycle. Never waste ♻️
m: An economy where products are reused, repaired and recycled instead of thrown away.
e: A phone company takes back old phones, recycles parts and uses them in new ones.
i: "A circular economy saves resources and cuts waste costs."

h: How one reel reaches 1 crore people overnight 🚀
m: Content made to spread fast as people share it with each other.
e: A funny brand reel gets shared so much that it reaches millions without paid ads.
i: "Virality cannot be guaranteed, but sharable ideas improve the chances."

h: Why banks ask you to 'keep something' for a loan 🔐
m: Something valuable you pledge to a lender, which they can take if you don't repay.
e: For a gold loan, the bank keeps your gold jewellery as collateral until you repay.
i: "Collateral lowers the lender's risk, so loans may be cheaper."

h: The best bosses work for their team 🙌
m: A leadership style where the leader focuses on helping the team grow and succeed.
e: A manager removes problems for her team and gives them credit for every success.
i: "Servant leaders build trust, so teams perform better."

h: Who stops big companies from bullying smaller ones? ⚖️
m: The government body that prevents unfair business practices and protects competition in India.
e: CCI fines companies that join together to fix prices or abuse their market power.
i: "Fair competition gives customers better prices and choices."

h: Being first isn't always winning. But it helps 🥇
m: The benefit a company gets by entering a market before competitors.
e: The first big e-commerce players built trust and delivery networks before rivals arrived.
i: "Being first helps only if you keep improving."
tm: Learning from the first one's mistakes.

h: From cotton farm to your T-shirt. A long journey 👕
m: The whole network of steps from raw materials to the final product in a customer's hands.
e: Cotton is grown, spun, woven, stitched, packed and shipped before you buy a T-shirt.
i: "A strong supply chain avoids delays and stock shortages."

h: Small budget. Big noise. Here's how 🦍
m: Low-cost, surprising marketing ideas that grab attention in public places.
e: A brand paints a giant 3D pothole on a road to promote road-safety tyres.
i: "Guerrilla marketing works best when the idea is clever, not expensive."

h: Your salary vanishes by the 20th? Read this 📝
m: Planning how much money you will earn, spend and save.
e: A student plans: Rs 8,000 for rent, Rs 4,000 for food, Rs 1,000 savings each month.
i: "A simple budget is the first step to financial freedom."

h: IQ gets you hired. EQ gets you promoted 🧠
m: The ability to understand and manage your own emotions and those of others.
e: A manager notices a team member is upset and talks to her privately instead of scolding her.
i: "High EQ helps in teamwork, leadership and handling pressure."

f: Securities and Exchange Board of India
h: The referee of India's stock market 🧑‍⚖️
m: The regulator that protects investors and oversees stock markets in India.
e: SEBI sets rules for IPOs and punishes people involved in share price fraud.
i: "SEBI's rules make markets safer for small investors."

h: Stop fighting rivals. Create a new market 🌊
m: Creating a new market space with little competition instead of competing in a crowded one.
e: A brand that made affordable premium-looking eyewear online found space big chains ignored.
i: "Blue ocean thinking asks: what can we offer that nobody else does?"

h: Why next-day delivery is a miracle of planning 🚚
m: Planning and managing the movement and storage of goods.
e: An e-commerce company plans warehouses and trucks so orders reach customers in 2 days.
i: "Good logistics is often the hidden reason companies win."

h: Why liquor brands sell 'soda' on TV 🥤
m: Advertising a banned product indirectly by promoting a different product with the same brand name.
e: Liquor brands in India advertise soda or music CDs under the same brand name.
i: "Surrogate ads are legally grey, so brands now face stricter rules."

h: Job loss. Hospital bill. Are you ready? 🛟
m: Money saved for sudden needs, usually enough for 3 to 6 months of expenses.
e: Ravi keeps Rs 1.5 lakh in a savings account only for emergencies.
i: "An emergency fund stops you from taking costly loans in a crisis."
tm: Money put to work for growth.

h: Two companies, same salary. Different vibe. Why? 🏢
m: The shared values, habits and behaviour that shape how work happens in a company.
e: In some companies anyone can question the boss in meetings. In others, nobody speaks.
i: "I ask about culture in interviews, because it decides daily happiness."

h: Every country has a bank for banks. India's is RBI 🏛️
m: A country's main bank that issues currency, controls money supply and regulates banks.
e: The RBI prints notes, manages interest rates and supervises all banks in India.
i: "An independent central bank keeps inflation under control."

h: What stops rivals from copying you? 🏰
m: A lasting advantage that protects a business from competitors.
e: A strong brand, a big user network or a patent can all be a company's moat.
i: "I would ask what our moat is before investing in growth."

h: Why some factories keep almost zero stock 🏭
m: A system where materials arrive exactly when needed for production, not earlier.
e: A car plant gets seats delivered a few hours before they are fitted.
i: "JIT cuts storage cost but needs very reliable suppliers."
tm: Keeping extra stock as a buffer.

h: Two brands, one product. Double the fans 🤝
m: Two brands joining to create one product or offer.
e: A bank and an airline launch a co-branded credit card that earns flight miles.
i: "Co-branding works when both brands share similar customers."

h: The cheapest way to protect your family 👨‍👩‍👧
m: Life insurance that pays a large amount to the family only if the person dies during the term.
e: A Rs 1 crore term plan for a 25-year-old can cost under Rs 1,000 a month.
i: "Term insurance gives maximum protection at the lowest cost."

h: Why companies take teams on trips and games 🧗
m: Activities that help team members trust and work better with each other.
e: A team goes trekking together, and later collaborates more easily at work.
i: "Real team building happens in daily work, not just one outing."

h: Not UPI. Not crypto. India's digital cash 📲
m: A digital form of currency issued directly by the RBI.
e: The RBI is piloting the e-rupee, which works like cash stored in a phone wallet.
i: "A digital rupee could make payments cheaper and easier to track."
tm: Private digital token, not legal tender.

h: Investors don't fund ideas. They fund this 📈
m: Proof that customers want your product, shown by users, sales or growth.
e: A startup with 10,000 paying users growing 20% every month has strong traction.
i: "Traction speaks louder than any pitch."

h: Only 3.4 mistakes in a million. That's the goal 🎯
m: A method to improve quality by reducing defects and variation in processes.
e: A company uses Six Sigma to cut billing errors from 5% to almost zero.
i: "Six Sigma makes quality measurable and steady."

h: From soap to shampoo with the same trusted name 🧴
m: Using a successful brand name to launch products in a new category.
e: A dairy brand famous for butter launches ice cream under the same name.
i: "Brand extension saves money, but a bad product can hurt the main brand."

h: One tax for the whole country. Here's how it works 🧾
m: A single tax on goods and services across India, replacing many older taxes.
e: Your restaurant bill shows GST added on the food price.
i: "GST made it easier to move goods between states."

h: Two teammates fighting? Here's the grown-up way 🤝
m: Solving disagreements in a calm, fair way that works for both sides.
e: A manager brings two arguing teammates together to agree on clear task divisions.
i: "I handle conflict by listening first and focusing on the problem, not the person."

h: Crores of Indians got their first bank account. How? 🏦
m: Making banking, credit and insurance available to everyone, including the poor.
e: Jan Dhan Yojana helped crores of people open zero-balance bank accounts.
i: "Financial inclusion brings poor households into the formal economy."

h: Clever tricks that grew apps to crores of users 🧪
m: Low-cost, creative experiments to grow users quickly.
e: An app gives you free credits for every friend who joins using your code.
i: "Growth hacks work best when the product itself is good."

h: Get 1% better every day. Japan's secret 🇯🇵
m: A Japanese approach of making small, continuous improvements every day.
e: Workers suggest small changes, like moving tools closer, that save minutes every day.
i: "Kaizen shows that small daily changes add up to big results."

h: That store's own brand? Made by someone else 🏷️
m: Products made by one company but sold under a retailer's own brand name.
e: Supermarket chains sell their own brand of rice and biscuits, made by other manufacturers.
i: "Private labels give retailers higher margins than branded goods."

h: Why your salary has less than promised 🤔
m: Tax cut by the payer before paying you, and deposited with the government.
e: A company cuts TDS from an employee's salary every month and pays it to the tax department.
i: "TDS spreads tax payment through the year instead of one big bill."

h: Doing everything yourself is not leadership 🧩
m: Giving tasks and authority to others so work gets done efficiently.
e: A team leader assigns the report to one member and the presentation to another.
i: "Good delegation grows the team and frees the leader for bigger work."

h: We import more than we export. Here's the word 🚢
m: When a country's imports of goods are worth more than its exports.
e: India's big oil and electronics imports often create a trade deficit.
i: "A trade deficit isn't always bad if imports help growth."

h: Every turn makes the next one easier 🎡
m: A cycle where each improvement feeds the next, making growth faster over time.
e: More sellers bring more choice, which brings more buyers, which brings more sellers.
i: "Building a flywheel takes time, but then growth becomes self-driven."

h: Why your customer care call may go to another city 📞
m: Hiring an outside company to do work that a business could do itself.
e: A bank outsources its customer support to a specialist call centre company.
i: "Outsourcing saves cost, but quality must be closely watched."

h: No shop. No middleman. Straight to your door 📦
m: Brands that sell directly to customers online instead of through shops.
e: Many new Indian brands sell mattresses, snacks and skincare only through their own websites.
i: "D2C gives brands customer data and better margins."

h: Sold a share for profit? The taxman wants a slice 📈
m: Profit made from selling an asset like shares, gold or property for more than you paid.
e: Buying shares at Rs 100 and selling at Rs 150 gives a capital gain of Rs 50 per share.
i: "Holding investments longer can reduce capital gains tax."

h: 'Send me an update every hour.' Sound familiar? 😩
m: When a manager controls every small detail of an employee's work.
e: A manager checks every email before it is sent and corrects tiny things.
i: "Micromanagement kills trust, so I prefer clear goals and regular check-ins."

h: Why imported iPhones cost more in India 📱
m: A tax on goods imported from other countries.
e: India's tariffs on imported electronics make some phones costlier here.
i: "Tariffs protect local industry but can raise prices for buyers."
tm: Limit on how much can be imported.

h: Groceries in 10 minutes. How is that even possible? ⏱️
m: Delivering everyday items within minutes from small nearby warehouses.
e: Apps deliver milk, bread and snacks in 10 to 15 minutes from 'dark stores' in your area.
i: "Quick commerce depends on dense neighbourhoods and tight logistics."

h: Why big global companies open offices in Bengaluru 🌏
m: An office set up by a foreign company in another country to do its own tech and business work.
e: Many global banks and tech firms run large GCCs in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune.
i: "GCCs are creating many high-quality jobs in India."

h: Order online, return in store. That's not luck 🔄
m: Giving customers one smooth experience across app, website and physical stores.
e: You check a shirt on an app, try it in the store and get the bill on WhatsApp.
i: "Omnichannel works when stock and data are linked across all channels."

h: Who checks if the company's numbers are honest? 🔎
m: An independent check of a company's accounts to confirm they are correct.
e: Every listed company's yearly accounts are checked by chartered accountant auditors.
i: "A clean audit builds trust with investors and lenders."

h: Different people, better ideas. Proven 🌈
m: Having people of different backgrounds and making sure all feel valued and heard.
e: A company hires from many states, genders and abilities, and makes sure all can speak up in meetings.
i: "Diverse teams make better decisions because they see more angles."

h: Self-reliant India: slogan or strategy? 🇮🇳
m: India's push to become self-reliant by making more goods and technology at home.
e: More defence equipment, toys and electronics are now made in India instead of imported.
i: "Self-reliance works best when Indian products are also globally competitive."

h: They own no cabs, no hotels. Yet they run the show 🚕
m: A business that brings many service providers onto one platform under one brand.
e: Cab apps don't own cars. They connect lakhs of drivers to riders.
i: "Aggregators scale fast because they don't own the assets."

h: Your data is valuable. Who's protecting it? 🛡️
m: People's right to control how their personal information is collected and used.
e: India's DPDP Act, 2023 sets rules for how companies handle personal data.
i: "Respecting data privacy builds customer trust."

h: How a factory biscuit reaches your village shop 🚚
m: The path a product takes from the maker to the final customer.
e: Biscuits go from factory to distributor to wholesaler to the kirana shop near you.
i: "Strong distribution is why some brands are available in every small town."
tm: The full flow, including raw materials.

h: Rakhi is a promise of protection. So is this 🛡️
m: Paying a small regular amount so a company covers you against a big loss.
e: A Rs 5 lakh health policy pays the hospital bill if someone in the family falls sick.
i: "Insurance is about protection first, not returns."

h: Every workplace in India must have this committee ⚖️
m: An Indian law that requires workplaces to prevent and address sexual harassment.
e: Companies with 10 or more employees must set up an Internal Committee to handle complaints.
i: "Knowing your rights under POSH makes workplaces safer for everyone."

h: Roads, ports, power: the economy's skeleton 🛣️
m: Basic facilities like roads, railways, power and internet that an economy needs to run.
e: New expressways cut travel time between cities, helping trade and tourism.
i: "Infrastructure spending creates jobs now and growth later."
tm: Things built on top, like services.

h: Lakhs of sellers, one app 🛍️
m: A platform where many independent sellers sell directly to buyers.
e: Small sellers from Surat sell sarees across India through online marketplaces.
i: "A marketplace succeeds when it builds trust between buyers and sellers."
tm: One brand selling its own goods.

h: That 'hard to cancel' subscription? It's on purpose 😠
m: Tricky design in apps or websites that pushes people into choices they didn't want.
e: A site adds travel insurance to your cart without asking, hoping you won't notice.
i: "Dark patterns may boost sales now but destroy trust later."

h: Half of India lives in villages. Smart brands know it 🌾
m: Marketing products specially to customers in villages and small towns.
e: Shampoo companies sold Rs 1 sachets so rural buyers could afford to try them.
i: "Rural marketing needs small packs, local language and wide distribution."

h: Sold but not paid yet. That money has a name 🧾
m: Money customers owe a business for goods or services already delivered.
e: A supplier delivers Rs 2 lakh of goods to a shop on 30 days' credit. That's receivable.
i: "High receivables can squeeze cash flow even when sales are good."

h: Unhappy at work? There's a proper way to complain 📨
m: A formal system for employees to raise complaints and get them solved.
e: An employee raises a pay issue through the HR portal and gets a response in 7 days.
i: "A fair grievance system stops small issues from becoming big ones."

h: When the government and companies build together 🤝
m: A project where the government and a private company share the cost, work and risk.
e: Many airports and highways in India are built and run under PPP models.
